sources.quote: PJ: *!ű (Ju. !ű, Kx. !úː, Kg. !ù ~ !ú, Gr. !úː, OK. !u ~ !o, Ek. !ú). ◊ Preserved in all daughter dialects. Ju. shows the rare extra high tone on this root, possibly an archaic feature. [p.28; abbreviations p.25: 'Ju. = Juǀ’hoan'; cf. p.23: 'Although some details of Proto-Ju and the phonetic laws that tie it to its modern descendants still remain poorly understood (mostly in the sphere of tonology and non-productive / fossilized nominal morphology), all the dialects are close enough to provide evidence for the basic phonetic shape of the protoforms']
sources.note: Treats Ju (incl. Juǀ'hoan) as lexically tonal with tone marked on every cited form; states that Proto-Ju tonology is still poorly understood (p.23), notes Juǀ'hoan's 'rare extra high tone' on !ű 'bone' (p.28), that 'tonal alternations actually exist in Ju' (p.39, on Doke's purely tonal ȕːm 'mountain' vs ūːm 'stone'), and reconstructs ultra-low tone plus breathiness for some roots (pp. 49, 55). No tone inventory or tonal analysis is given.

sources.quote: There are four tone levels, but only six of the predicted tonal patterns are attested on verb roots. Verbs bear all four level tones, plus two of the three possible combinations of rising tones. [p. 2] ... I argue that this disparity arises because the tone bearing unit being [sic] is the mora. [p. 7] ... Perhaps footing is not relevant in this language, since it is a tonal language, and there is little evidence for the presence of feet. [p. 14]

sources.note: Tone: refines the catalog's bare 'lexical-tone' class. Four level tones on verb roots, labelled SL (super-low), L, H, SH (super-high), table (2) p. 3; roots are monotonal (SL SL, L L, H H, SH SH) or bitonal rising (SL L, L H); H SH rising is very rare and only on nouns; one falling pattern HL only on loanwords (nouns); SH SH only on monosyllabic roots (pp. 2-3). Tone bearing unit is the mora; phonetic contour tones decompose into two level tones each linked to a mora (pp. 7-8); a constraint allows no more than one tone per mora (p. 1); 'There is no tone spread or tone reassociation' (p. 1); 't

tone.quote: This study presents the results of an investigation of the fundamental frequency of vowels following guttural clicks in Ju/hoansi. ... The results here show that voicing only lowers fundamental frequency when the release phase of a consonant is voiced as is the case for the voiced aspirated clicks, and not when there is only closure voicing, as is found in the case of the voiced epiglottalized clicks.
